finding.claim: Any authenticated user can delete any project because the DELETE route ignores the result of the authorized() predicate.
finding.source: req.params.id (api.js:17) and the caller's session via req.user

trace.note: Loads the project named by the URL parameter.
Calls authorized(req.user, project); the return value is discarded.
authorized() returns a boolean and never throws, so it cannot block the request.
Deletes the project regardless of ownership or admin status.

finding.guards_checked: Only guard on the path is authorized() at api.js:18, which is a predicate with no enforcement. The correct helper authorize() (api.js:4, throws on failure) is not used on this route. No other middleware in this file applies to the route. Assumes req.user is set by upstream authentication, which is not in this directory.

verdict.guard_found: The only check on the route is authorized() at api.js:18, a boolean predicate (api.js:12-14) whose result is discarded as a bare statement, so it enforces nothing. The throwing helper authorize() (api.js:4-10) is not called on this route. No other middleware exists: api.js is the only file in the directory. Upstream req.user population is outside the directory and is assumed, not verified.
verdict.reason: The DELETE handler at api.js:18 calls authorized(req.user, project) and ignores its boolean return, so the delete at api.js:19 runs for any caller who reaches the route with a valid req.user, which is any authenticated user per the stated attacker model. Trace is accurate; one nuance is that authorized() at api.js:13 would throw a TypeError (a 500, no delete) if the project lookup returns undefined, which does not change the verdict.

finding.claim: Nonexistent project IDs cause an unhandled TypeError instead of a 404, creating an existence oracle and possibly leaking stack traces.
finding.source: req.params.id for a nonexistent project (api.js:17, api.js:24)
finding.sink: project.ownerId dereference in authorize()/authorized() at api.js:5 and api.js:13, reached via api.js:18 and api.js:25

trace.note: store.projects.get(id) returns undefined for an unknown ID.
authorized(req.user, undefined) is called without a null check.
The PUT route has the same missing null check, reached through authorize() at api.js:25.

finding.guards_checked: No null or existence check on either route. Whether stack traces leak depends on the app's error handler, which is not in this directory. Severity is low: this is not a direct authorization bypass.

verdict.guard_found: none. No existence check at api.js:17-18 or api.js:24-25. The authorized() call at api.js:18 is a bare statement whose result is discarded, and authorize() at api.js:25 has no null check before resource.ownerId at api.js:5. The error-handler behavior that would decide stack-trace leakage is not in this directory.
verdict.reason: For an unknown ID, store.projects.get returns undefined (api.js:17), and api.js:13 (via api.js:18) and api.js:5 (via api.js:25) dereference resource.ownerId with no null check, so any caller that reaches these routes gets a TypeError rather than a 404, which is a real existence oracle at low severity. Separately, api.js:18 discards authorized()'s result, so DELETE /projects/:id has no ownership check at all, a much more serious authorization gap that the candidate did not report.

finding.claim: The rename route stores req.body.name with no type, length or content validation and returns the full project object, so stored XSS or injection is possible if the name is rendered unsafely elsewhere.
finding.source: req.body.name in the PUT /projects/:id/name request body (api.js:26)
finding.sink: project.name assignment at api.js:26, then res.json(project) at api.js:27, and any downstream rendering of the name (not in this directory)

trace.note: req.body.name is assigned directly to project.name with no validation.
The full project object, including the stored name, is returned as JSON.

finding.guards_checked: Ownership is enforced by authorize() at api.js:25, so this is not an authorization issue. There is no input validation or sanitization in this file. Body-size limits and rendering behavior are outside this directory. This is a candidate only; exploitability depends on code I cannot see.

verdict.guard_found: authorize() at api.js:25 (throws a 403 for non-owner, non-admin, so the bare call still aborts the handler before the write at api.js:26). No input validation or sanitization on req.body.name in this directory. res.json at api.js:27 sets an application/json response, so it is not itself an XSS sink.
verdict.reason: The trace matches api.js:26-27 and the write is only reachable by the project owner or an admin (authorize at api.js:25 throws otherwise), but whether a stored name is exploitable depends on rendering code outside this directory, so the candidate's own caveat holds and it cannot be confirmed or refuted from api.js alone.
